doc.title: Jason Palmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2025

title: The role of jazz in society
summary: Palmer says jazz tells the truth of individual experience, is social and intergenerational, and must be supported amid arts defunding.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yeah. All right. I’ve got a question I’ve been working on and maybe you can help me actually just form it, but it seems that jazz has had differing and changing roles in society, if we think back in its very early days it was “new” music, then it became really high entertainment pop music, sort of in the swing era. In the ‘50s you had sort of bebop characters and the Dizzy Gillespie sort of persona. Some civil rights connections in the ‘60s. This is all my own opinion, but do you feel that jazz has a role in society, American society now? What is the role of jazz?

Yeah I think it has the role to tell the truth about, you know, the individual’s experience. The collective experience of, you know, whoever the artist is and where they are geographically, regionally, and also to be able to tell the story and have what you have to present be something that you can share with people. I think this music is a social music. It’s a music that’s meant to be, you know, played, for people, you know with people. And yeah I think that’s something that we can really benefit from in terms of like really knowing what the possibilities of playing an instrument in a creative way can be. That’s why I don’t think this music will ever go away because the creative aspect of it will always draw people in to want to play. Even if there are no gigs. You know people will find a way to make their own gigs, make their own possibilities. Go play on the porch. You know there are porch-fests everywhere up in New England you know. There were some in my neighborhood when I was living in Boston you know. So there’s like a very local component that I think needs to be grown and nurtured, especially when you look at all the defunding that’s happened with the arts organizations and everything that’s going on now. I think we’re really going to have to really show the importance of playing music together. It’s just as important as throwing a basketball or passing something. The importance of cooperation, teamwork, listening and building and getting better and

development, that’s all in this type of music. And also there are so many things that we can learn about it because it’s intergenerational. You know I could go and play with 15- year-olds. I played with a young tenor player last night named Emilio Modeste. I mean he’s the spitting image of — like I thought I was playing next to Wayne Shorter and he’s probably half my age. You know and then I played with Sharon Jones, the great singer that’s in her seventies. And so I think that aspect of it, the social aspect and the history of it along with what we can contribute to it, you know there’s always something new that we can contribute to it because there’s always new stories that have a soundtrack to them. You know and we can also write based on history. You know and sometimes you know you put out projects and it informs people of the history because you just put out a project and it informs them. Like I did a project on the stolen artwork from the Isabella Stewart Gardner museum. I wrote a piece for every piece of art that was stolen. And so —
